title: Who made it, and who said what
lede: Titles and dates are as stated in the cited filings, releases and articles. Later careers are listed only where a source covers them.

people.name: Douglas L. Mason
people.role: Founder, chief executive officer and president of Clearly Canadian
people.text: Mason founded the Clearly Canadian business and product line in 1986, according to the company’s annual report for 2002.[^6] A 2005 company release credits him with launching Jolt Cola under license in 1985, introducing the Clearly Canadian brand in 1987 and leading the team that launched Quenchers, Orbitz and Reebok Fitness Water.[^25] In April 1997 he called the response to the U.S. launch of Orbitz “overwhelmingly positive” in the Canadian launch release.[^8]
people.later: Replaced as chief executive when Brent Lokash was named president in October 2005; the release said Mason would continue to play an active role.[^25]

people.name: Jonathan J. Cronin
people.role: Marketing executive; vice-president, marketing from January 1997
people.text: Cronin joined Clearly Canadian in the fall of 1993.[^6] He was the company’s voice on Orbitz. He told AP in 1996 that the aim was to make whoever brought it into a room the center of attention for a few moments. In August 1998 he told Strategy that Orbitz was still weird but no longer new.[^1][^4]
people.later: Transferred to the company’s U.S. operating subsidiary in December 1998.[^6]

people.name: Brent Lokash
people.text: The company named Lokash president on October 4, 2005, replacing chief executive Douglas Mason.[^25] In February 2007, announcing the purchase of DMR Food Corporation, he said the acquisition would nearly double top-line revenues.[^34]

people.name: Bobby Genovese
people.text: BevNET named Genovese as chief executive in May 2008, when he told shareholders that Clearly Canadian had grown revenue in 2007 for the first time in over 10 years.[^33] The article says BG Capital Group, led by Genovese, became a controlling shareholder in Clearly Canadian about three years earlier.[^33]

people.name: Jesse Wolff
people.role: Chemical engineer who helped develop Orbitz
people.text: Science World quoted Wolff in 1996 describing the liquid as a fluid gel made from ingredients similar to those in Jell-O.[^9]

people.name: William Chalupa
people.role: Fluid-gel expert quoted by Science World
people.text: He conceded to Science World that gravity does indeed act on Orbitz.[^9] A William F. Chalupa is named as an inventor on Bush Boake Allen’s patent application for suspending inclusions; we could not confirm that he is the same person.[^12]

people.name: Bill O’Leary
people.text: In April 1997 he said his company was the sole, exclusive distributor of Orbitz and Clearly Canadian beverages in the Washington region and had carried Orbitz for six weeks.[^3]

people.name: Dirk Van Stralen
people.text: The April 1997 launch release says he drew comics for the Planet Orbitz site.[^8]

people.name: Robert R. Khan
people.text: Fast Company reported in October 2024 that Khan acquired the Clearly Canadian company in 2012.[^24]

people.name: Casey Howe
people.role: Vice-president of marketing, Clearly Canadian, in October 2024
people.text: Fast Company quoted Howe in October 2024 saying the brand was on track to sell around 45 million bottles that year, a company projection.[^24]
